entities.summary: Pope Miltiades, also known as Melchiades the African, was the bishop of Rome from 311 to his death on 10 or 11 January 314. During his pontificate, Emperor Constantine the Great issued the Edict of Milan (313), giving Christianity legal status within the Roman Empire. The pope also received the palace of Empress Fausta where the Lateran Palace, the papal seat and residence of the papal administration, would be built. At the Lateran Council, during the schism with the Church of Carthage, Miltiades convened a council to address the schism, which ultimately resulted in the condemnation of Donatus of Besair. The council also established the position of the bishop of Carthage, a crucial step in the development of the papacy's authority. This marked a significant turning point in the history of Christianity, as it solidified the papacy's role as the central authority of the Church. As a result, Miltiades played a pivotal role in shaping the course of Christian history, leaving a lasting legacy that continues to influence the Church's development to this day. Miltiades' commitment to unity and authority helped to establish the papacy as a powerful force in Western Christianity, paving the way for the Church's future growth and development. The Edict of Milan, issued during his pontificate, marked a significant milestone in the history of religious freedom, as it granted Christians the right to practice their faith openly within the Roman Empire. This marked a major turning point in the history of religious tolerance, as it set a precedent for future laws and policies that would protect the rights of religious minorities. The Lateran Palace, built during Miltiades' reign, became a symbol of the papacy's power and influence, serving as a center of spiritual and temporal authority for centuries to come. The council's condemnation of Donatus of Besair also had significant implications for the development of the Donatist movement, which would go on to shape the theology and politics of the Church for centuries to come. As a result, Miltiades' leadership during this period had a profound impact on the course of Christian history, shaping the Church's institutions, theology, and practices in lasting ways.
